chunks: Ali ibn al-Hasan from Hammad from Hariz from Abu Basir from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) that he said:

I heard him say: 'There is no zakat in the wealth of the orphan, and no salat upon him, and there is no zakat upon all his produce from palm trees or crops or any produce, even if it increases; he is not liable for zakat for what has passed, nor for what is to come, until he reaches maturity. When he reaches maturity, one zakat becomes due upon him, and he is like the rest of the people.'

This is not contradictory to the first narration, because he (peace be upon him) said: 'There is no zakat upon all his produce,' and we do not say that there is zakat upon all his produce; rather, it is obligatory upon the four types, which are dates, raisins, wheat, and barley. The orphans were singled out with this ruling because others are recommended to pay zakat from other grains, but this is not the case for the wealth of orphans; therefore, they were singled out in the mention.

Saad ibn Abdillah from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Muhammad ibn al-Qasim ibn al-Fudayl al-Basri said: I wrote to Abu al-Hasan al-Rida (peace be upon him) asking him about the executor who pays the zakat of fitrah on behalf of the orphans if they have wealth, and he wrote: 'There is no zakat upon the wealth of the orphan.'
As for that which indicates that the insane are included with them in this ruling, it is what was narrated:
ai.seo_question: Is zakat obligatory on the wealth of orphans before they reach maturity?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi contextualizes this ruling by clarifying that the exemption applies specifically to the four primary zakatable produce types, distinguishing orphans from adults who are merely recommended (mandub) to pay on other grains. The text further extends this principle to include the insane (majanin), as evidenced by Imam al-Rida’s written response confirming no zakat is due on their wealth, thereby establishing a consistent legal precedent for dependents lacking full financial agency.
